t: Lexicographically Smallest String After Deleting Duplicate Characters
o: You may delete an occurrence of any letter that currently appears at least twice; letters appearing once can never be removed. From "aaccb" the reachable minimal answers keep every distinct letter at least once, and the best is "aacb". For "baa" the best is "ba" (shorter beats longer on a common prefix). So the task is: pick a subsequence that contains every distinct letter of s at least once and is lexicographically smallest. With n up to 1e5 we need a linear greedy.
k: Any subsequence that keeps at least one copy of each distinct letter is achievable: delete unwanted occurrences from right to left, so a deleted letter always has surviving copies.
The answer is the lexicographically smallest such subsequence, solvable with the classic monotonic-stack greedy using each letter's last occurrence.

a.i: Iterate left to right keeping a result stack. When the current char c is smaller than the stack top t, pop t if t occurs again later (last[t] > i), because keeping a later t is always at least as good. Skip a char already in the stack (keeping the earliest copy is optimal since duplicates never help). The stack ends as the smallest subsequence covering all letters.
s: Precompute last occurrence of each letter.
For each char: skip if already used; otherwise pop stack tops that are larger and recur later; push and mark used.
a.t: O(n) — each character is pushed and popped at most once

w: Key modeling step: realize the answer must contain every distinct letter at least once (letters with one occurrence can never be deleted, and removing all copies of a letter is impossible). Then it is the standard smallest-subsequence-covering-alphabet greedy. Pitfall: forgetting the `already used` skip, which would duplicate letters. Follow-up: largest such string (flip comparisons).
